claim: Type II topoisomerases manage DNA supercoiling and aid chromosome segregation using a complex, ATP-dependent duplex strand passage mechanism.
source: Type II topoisomerases manage DNA supercoiling and aid chromosome segregation using a complex, ATP-dependent duplex strand passage mechanism.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract describing the general function of type II topoisomerases, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Topo VI is a prototypical type IIB topoisomerase that comprises two Top6A and two Top6B protomers.
source: Topo VI, a prototypical type IIB topoisomerase, comprises two Top6A and two Top6B protomers
evidence: This statement describes the structural composition of topo VI, which is established knowledge cited in the introduction.

claim: Top6B harbors the ATPase activity of topo VI.
source: Top6B, which harbors the ATPase activity of topo VI
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Top6B recognizes and exploits DNA crossings present in supercoiled DNA to stimulate subunit dimerization by ATP.
source: we show that Top6B, which harbors the ATPase activity of topo VI, recognizes and exploits the DNA crossings present in supercoiled DNA to stimulate subunit dimerization by ATP.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by multiple biochemical experiments including FRET assays and ATPase activity measurements.

claim: Top6B self-association induces extensive DNA bending, which is needed to support duplex cleavage by Top6A.
source: Top6B self-association in turn induces extensive DNA bending, which is needed to support duplex cleavage by Top6A.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by FRET-based DNA bending assays and cleavage experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Type IIA topoisomerases utilize a 'two-gate' mechanism.
source: The type IIA subfamily of topoisomerases, which are principally used in bacteria and eukaryotes, utilize a so-called 'two-gate' mechanism (Roca et al., 1996; Roca and Wang, 1994; Roca and Wang, 1992)
evidence: This statement describes an established mechanism for type IIA topoisomerases and is supported by citations.

claim: In the two-gate mechanism, one DNA duplex (T-segment) is captured by one half of the enzyme, actively passed through a second protein-bound DNA duplex (G-segment), and expelled through the other end of the enzyme.
source: in which one DNA duplex (termed the transport- or 'T'-segment) is captured by one half of the enzyme, actively passed through a second, protein-bound DNA duplex (the gate- or 'G'-segment), and expelled through the other end of the enzyme.
evidence: This describes the established two-gate mechanism of type IIA topoisomerases, supported by citations.

claim: T-segment capture is regulated by ATP-dependent closure of the ATP-gate subunit dimer interface.
source: T-segment capture is regulated by the ATP-dependent closure of one subunit dimer interface (Roca and Wang, 1992; Wigley et al., 1991), referred to as the 'ATP-gate'
evidence: This statement describes a regulatory mechanism supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A pair of catalytic tyrosine residues responsible for G-segment cleavage and opening reside in the DNA-gate.
source: while a pair of catalytic tyrosine residues responsible for G-segment cleavage and opening reside in a second, separable subunit-subunit contact point termed the 'DNA-gate' (Berger et al., 1996; Morais Cabral et al., 1997; Morrison and Cozzarelli, 1979; Tse et al., 1980).
evidence: This describes the location and function of catalytic residues, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Repeated cycles of ATP binding and hydrolysis allow for processive removal of multiple DNA crossings in most type II topoisomerases.
source: In most instances, repeated cycles of ATP binding and hydrolysis allow for the processive removal of multiple DNA crossings.
evidence: This describes general behavior of type II topoisomerases based on established knowledge.

claim: ATP use by type II topoisomerases has been proposed to prevent inappropriate formation of potentially cytotoxic DNA breaks.
source: The use of ATP by type II topoisomerases in general has been proposed to serve as a mechanism for preventing the inappropriate formation of potentially cytotoxic DNA breaks (Bates et al., 2011)
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by a citation.

claim: The molecular basis for coupling between ATP turnover and DNA cleavage has remained enigmatic for the type II topoisomerase superfamily.
source: however, the molecular basis for the coupling between ATP turnover and DNA cleavage has remained enigmatic for the superfamily as a whole.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Type IIB topoisomerases share evolutionarily conserved catalytic elements with type IIA counterparts but are structurally distinct.
source: The type IIB topoisomerases, which are exemplified by DNA topoisomerase VI (topo VI) (Bergerat et al., 1997; Bergerat et al., 1994; Forterre et al., 2007), share evolutionarily conserved catalytic elements with their type IIA counterparts but are structurally distinct (Corbett and Berger, 2003; Nichols et al., 1999).
evidence: This describes the relationship between type IIA and IIB topoisomerases, supported by citations.

claim: Topo VI comprises an A2B2 heterotetramer formed by two Top6A and two Top6B subunits.
source: Topo VI comprises an A2B2 heterotetramer formed by two Top6A and two Top6B subunits
evidence: This describes the structural composition of topo VI, supported by citations.

claim: Top6A forms a U-shaped dimer that serves as the DNA-gate for G-segment cleavage and opening.
source: Top6A forms a 'U'-shaped dimer that serves as the DNA-gate for G-segment cleavage and opening (Bergerat et al., 1997; Nichols et al., 1999)
evidence: This describes the structure and function of Top6A, supported by citations.

claim: Top6B constitutes the ATP-gate and dimerizes in response to nucleotide binding.
source: while Top6B constitutes the ATP-gate and dimerizes in response to nucleotide binding (Corbett and Berger, 2003).
evidence: This describes the function of Top6B, supported by a citation.

claim: Topo VI is thought to serve as the primary topoisomerase for DNA decatenation and supercoil relaxation in archaea.
source: Topo VI is thought to serve as the primary topoisomerase for DNA decatenation and supercoil relaxation in archaea and is required for endoreduplication and cell growth in plants (Bergerat et al., 1997; Bergerat et al., 1994; Hartung et al., 2002; Sugimoto-Shirasu et al., 2002; Yin et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes the biological role of topo VI, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Topo VI is required for endoreduplication and cell growth in plants.
source: Topo VI is thought to serve as the primary topoisomerase for DNA decatenation and supercoil relaxation in archaea and is required for endoreduplication and cell growth in plants (Bergerat et al., 1997; Bergerat et al., 1994; Hartung et al., 2002; Sugimoto-Shirasu et al., 2002; Yin et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes the biological role of topo VI in plants, supported by citations.

claim: The type IIB topoisomerase scaffold has been co-opted to serve as machinery for introducing double-strand DNA breaks to initiate meiotic recombination in eukaryotes.
source: Interestingly, the type IIB topoisomerase scaffold has been co-opted to serve as the machinery responsible for introducing double-strand DNA breaks to initiate meiotic recombination in eukaryotes (Bergerat et al., 1997; Keeney et al., 1997; Robert et al., 2016; Vrielynck et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes an evolutionary adaptation of the type IIB scaffold, supported by citations.

claim: The ATPase region is generally well-preserved between type IIA and type IIB topoisomerases.
source: The ATPase region is generally well-preserved between type IIA and type IIB topoisomerases, with the exception of an additional helix-two-turn-helix (H2TH) domain of unknown function found in topo VI and topo VIII (Bergerat et al., 1997; Corbett and Berger, 2003; Gadelle et al., 2014; Wigley et al., 1991).
evidence: This describes structural conservation between type IIA and IIB topoisomerases, supported by citations.

claim: Topo VI and topo VIII contain an additional H2TH domain of unknown function not found in type IIA topoisomerases.
source: The ATPase region is generally well-preserved between type IIA and type IIB topoisomerases, with the exception of an additional helix-two-turn-helix (H2TH) domain of unknown function found in topo VI and topo VIII (Bergerat et al., 1997; Corbett and Berger, 2003; Gadelle et al., 2014; Wigley et al., 1991).
evidence: This describes a structural difference between type IIA and IIB topoisomerases, supported by citations.

claim: Top6A lacks a C-gate dimerization domain present in type IIA enzymes.
source: One consequence of this rearrangement is that Top6A lacks a third subunit-subunit interface present in the type IIA enzymes, the 'C-gate' dimerization domain, which is thought to help mitigate the risk of aberrant double-strand break formation (Bates et al., 2011; Berger et al., 1996; Nichols et al., 1999; Roca, 2004).
evidence: This describes a structural difference between Top6A and type IIA topoisomerases, supported by citations.

claim: The C-gate dimerization domain in type IIA enzymes is thought to help mitigate the risk of aberrant double-strand break formation.
source: One consequence of this rearrangement is that Top6A lacks a third subunit-subunit interface present in the type IIA enzymes, the 'C-gate' dimerization domain, which is thought to help mitigate the risk of aberrant double-strand break formation (Bates et al., 2011; Berger et al., 1996; Nichols et al., 1999; Roca, 2004).
evidence: This describes a proposed function of the C-gate, supported by citations.

claim: Type IIB topoisomerases appear to have evolved a stringent mechanism for controlling strand scission by Top6A that represses transesterase activity until ATP productively binds to Top6B.
source: To compensate for the loss of this element, type IIB topoisomerases appear to have evolved a stringent mechanism for controlling strand scission by Top6A that represses transesterase activity until ATP productively binds to Top6B (Buhler et al., 1998; Buhler et al., 2001).
evidence: This describes a regulatory mechanism in type IIB topoisomerases, supported by citations.

claim: Spo11, a paralog of Top6A used in meiotic recombination, is thought to require activation for DNA cleavage.
source: however, given that Spo11, a paralog of Top6A used in meiotic recombination, is also thought to require activation for DNA cleavage, aspects of this control mechanism may be broadly conserved (Lam and Keeney, 2014).
evidence: This describes a proposed regulatory mechanism for Spo11, supported by a citation.

claim: Topo VI discriminates between linear and supercoiled DNA using an extensive DNA binding interface that specifically recognizes DNA crossings.
source: We find that topo VI discriminates between linear and supercoiled DNA using an extensive and unanticipated DNA binding interface that specifically recognizes DNA crossings.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by DNA binding and competition experiments shown in Figures 1 and 5.

claim: Both gate closure and ATP hydrolysis by Top6B as well as transesterase activity by Top6A require engagement along the entire DNA binding interface.
source: Both gate closure and ATP hydrolysis by Top6B as well as transesterase activity by Top6A require engagement along this entire interface.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experiments with mutants affecting different regions of the DNA binding interface.

claim: Three conserved, positively charged regions on Top6B sense both DNA bends and crossings present in supercoiled substrates.
source: Site-directed mutagenesis studies show that three conserved, positively charged regions on Top6B sense both the DNA bends and crossings present in supercoiled substrates
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by mutagenesis experiments and functional assays shown in Figures 3-7.

claim: Three conserved, positively charged regions on Top6B serve to couple DNA crossing binding to B-subunit dimerization, nucleotide turnover, and DNA strand scission.
source: Site-directed mutagenesis studies show that three conserved, positively charged regions on Top6B sense both the DNA bends and crossings present in supercoiled substrates and further serve to couple the binding of DNA crossings to B-subunit dimerization, nucleotide turnover, and DNA strand scission.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by mutagenesis experiments and functional assays shown in Figures 3-7.

claim: The affinity of topo VI for fluorescein-labeled duplex DNAs increases with length from 20 bp to 70 bp.
source: These experiments showed that whereas a 20 bp duplex binds relatively weakly to topo VI, apparent affinity increases with length, plateauing between 40 and 70 bp (Figure 1A, Figure 1—source datas 2–3).
evidence: This finding is supported by fluorescence anisotropy experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Topo VI shows a ~60-fold preference for supercoiled DNA compared to sheared salmon-sperm DNA.
source: Based on these measurements, topo VI showed a ~60-fold preference for supercoiled DNA (KI,app = 0.6 ± 0.3 nM) compared to sheared salmon-sperm DNA (KI,app = 39.3 ± 2.6 nM) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This finding is supported by competitive binding experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Topo VI operates by a principally distributive mechanism.
source: Collectively, these findings demonstrate that topo VI operates by a principally distributive mechanism, whereby once a DNA crossing is resolved by strand passage, the enzyme will tend to dissociate from the substrate before acting on a new crossing and/or bent DNA segment.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by plasmid relaxation timecourse and chase experiments shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Topo VI shows negligible basal ATPase activity and requires DNA substrate addition to hydrolyze ATP.
source: Topo VI showed negligible basal ATPase activity, and required the addition of a DNA substrate to hydrolyze ATP.
evidence: This finding is supported by ATPase activity measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Incubation of topo VI with supercoiled DNA produces a ~5-fold increase in catalytic efficiency (kcat,app/Km,app) over that for sheared salmon-sperm DNA.
source: Incubation with supercoiled DNA produced the maximal observed rate of hydrolysis (and decreased the Km,app for ATP), resulting in a ~5-fold increase in catalytic efficiency (kcat,app/Km,app) over that for sheared salmon-sperm DNA.
evidence: This finding is supported by ATPase activity measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Supercoiled DNA is more effective than linear substrates in activating ATP turnover by topo VI.
source: The observation that supercoiled DNA is more effective than linear substrates in activating ATP turnover indicates that topo VI not only interrogates DNA for specific topological features, but that its activity is potentiated when such features are recognized.
evidence: This conclusion is based on ATPase activity measurements comparing supercoiled and linear DNA substrates.

claim: The addition of sheared salmon-sperm DNA and supercoiled DNA to topo VI leads to minor but reproducible increases in FRET efficiency.
source: The addition of sheared salmon-sperm DNA and to a greater extent supercoiled DNA, led to minor but reproducible increases in FRET efficiency (Figures 2C, 0 min time-point), suggesting that DNA binding alone alters the conformation of Top6B in the holoenzyme.
evidence: This finding is supported by FRET experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The addition of AMPPNP to topo VI leads to larger FRET responses, with FRET efficiency increasing much more rapidly with supercoiled DNA compared to linear sheared salmon-sperm DNA.
source: By comparison, the addition of AMPPNP led to larger FRET responses, and FRET efficiency increased much more rapidly with supercoiled DNA compared to linear sheared salmon-sperm DNA.
evidence: This finding is supported by FRET experiments shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: AMPPNP alone produces detectable but minor FRET changes when DNA is omitted, indicating that duplex binding is needed for ATPase domain dimerization.
source: AMPPNP alone produced detectable but minor FRET changes when DNA was omitted, indicating that duplex binding is needed for ATPase domain dimerization (Figure 2D, 120 min time-point).
evidence: This finding is supported by FRET experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Unlike type IIA topoisomerases, whose ATPase regions efficiently dimerize in the absence of DNA, topo VI utilizes DNA geometries presented by supercoiled substrates to help favor nucleotide-dependent conformational changes associated with strand passage.
source: In conjunction with the ATPase data, these observations show that – unlike type IIA topoisomerases, whose ATPase regions efficiently dimerize in the absence of DNA ([Gubaev and Klostermeier, 2011; Roca and Wang, 1992] and Figure 2—figure supplement 3) – topo VI utilizes the DNA geometries presented by supercoiled substrates to help favor nucleotide-dependent conformational changes associated with strand passage.
evidence: This conclusion is based on FRET experiments comparing topo VI to ScTop2, supported by data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Both sets of KGRR and Stalk/WKxY mutants (neutral and acidic) are completely unable to relax supercoiled substrate.
source: Both sets of KGRR and Stalk/WKxY mutants (neutral and acidic) proved completely unable to relax supercoiled substrate.
evidence: This finding is supported by supercoil relaxation assays shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both sets of mutations to the H2TH region lead to enzymes that can relax supercoiled DNA, but with ~20–30 fold lower efficiency than native topo VI.
source: By contrast, both sets of mutations to the H2TH region led to enzymes that were able to relax supercoiled DNA, but with ~20–30 fold lower efficiency than native topo VI.
evidence: This finding is supported by supercoil relaxation assays shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The KGRR loop and the Stalk/WKxY region are essential components for topo VI function.
source: Collectively, these findings show that the KGRR loop and the Stalk/WKxY region are essential components for topo VI function, but that the H2TH domain, while important, is not strictly required for strand passage.
evidence: This conclusion is based on supercoil relaxation assays with mutants shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The H2TH domain, while important, is not strictly required for strand passage by topo VI.
source: Collectively, these findings show that the KGRR loop and the Stalk/WKxY region are essential components for topo VI function, but that the H2TH domain, while important, is not strictly required for strand passage.
evidence: This conclusion is based on supercoil relaxation assays with mutants shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No DNA-stimulated ATP turnover was observed for either of the Stalk/WKxY mutants.
source: No DNA-stimulated ATP turnover was observed for either of the Stalk/WKxY mutants.
evidence: This finding is supported by ATPase activity measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The H2THAAA and H2THEEE mutants show similar levels of ATP hydrolysis stimulation by both DNA substrates as compared to wildtype topo VI.
source: Interestingly, the H2THAAA and H2THEEE mutants, which exhibited large defects in strand passage, showed similar levels of ATP hydrolysis stimulation by both DNA substrates as compared to wildtype topo VI.
evidence: This finding is supported by ATPase activity measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The KGRRAAA and KGRREEE mutants show no additional ATP turnover on sheared salmon-sperm DNA, but show increased maximal rate of DNA-stimulated ATP hydrolysis on supercoiled DNA compared to wildtype enzyme.
source: Moreover, whereas no additional ATP turnover was observed for the KGRRAAA and KGRREEE mutants on sheared salmon-sperm DNA, both variants showed an increased maximal rate of DNA-stimulated ATP hydrolysis compared to the wild-type enzyme on supercoiled DNA (albeit with a more weakly coupled response to DNA concentration than wildtype topo VI or the H2TH mutants as judged by Kstim,DNA).
evidence: This finding is supported by ATPase activity measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The abrogation of strand passage activity by the KGRR loop mutants stems in part from a loss of an essential DNA-sensing motif required to carry out strand passage.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that the abrogation of strand passage activity by the KGRR loop mutants stems in part from a loss of an essential DNA-sensing motif required to carry out strand passage.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined results of strand passage and ATPase assays with KGRR mutants.

claim: Mutations to the H2TH domain appear to largely decouple strand passage from ATP hydrolysis, yet do not appreciably alter the DNA dependence of ATPase activity.
source: Mutations to the H2TH domain additionally appear to largely decouple strand passage from ATP hydrolysis, yet do not appreciably alter the DNA dependence of ATPase activity.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined results of strand passage and ATPase assays with H2TH mutants.

claim: The H2TH domain plays a role in facilitating A- and B-subunit coordination to minimize futile cycling.
source: This result implies a role for the H2TH domain in facilitating A- and B-subunit coordination to minimize futile cycling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that H2TH mutants decouple strand passage from ATP hydrolysis.

claim: Both Stalk/WKxY mutants are compromised for DNA binding overall, with the magnitude of binding defects more severe for the acidic substitutions.
source: Both Stalk/WKxY mutants were compromised for DNA binding overall (as judged by the maximum observed changes in anisotropy), with the magnitude of the binding defects proving more severe for the acidic substitutions.
evidence: This finding is supported by DNA binding experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The Stalk/WKxY region of Top6B is an important DNA-binding interface.
source: This finding highlights the Stalk/WKxY region of Top6B as an important DNA-binding interface, a finding that helps explain both why the binding affinity of topo VI is higher for DNAs whose length exceeds what is necessary to bind a Top6A dimer alone and why mutations in this region lead to defects in both strand passage and ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This conclusion is based on DNA binding experiments with Stalk/WKxY mutants shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The KGRR loop and H2TH domain mutants show either no change or only a moderate decrease in DNA affinity for 60 and 70 bp duplexes compared to wildtype topo VI.
source: By comparison, the KGRR loop and the H2TH domain mutants showed either no change or only a moderate decrease (for the 60 and 70 bp duplexes) in DNA affinity compared to wildtype topo VI, suggesting that these regions potentially contribute a more peripheral or secondary site of DNA binding.
evidence: This finding is supported by DNA binding experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The H2THEEE and both KGRR substitutions result in a ~10–20 fold decrease of the overall affinity of topo VI for supercoiled DNA.
source: The H2THAAA substitution minimally affected supercoiled DNA binding, whereas the H2THEEE and both KGRR substitutions resulted in a ~10–20 fold decrease of the overall affinity of topo VI for supercoiled DNA, with KGRREEE showing a greater defect than KGRRAAA.
evidence: This finding is supported by competitive binding experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Both KGRR substitutions adversely impact the binding of random linear DNA compared to wild type.
source: Both KGRR substitutions adversely impacted the binding of random linear DNA compared to wild type as well, a result concordant with this mutant's negligible ATPase activity on sheared salmon-sperm DNA and which further suggests that this set of substitutions may ablate a secondary DNA-binding site on the holoenzyme.
evidence: This finding is supported by competitive binding experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Both the KGRR loop and H2TH domain contribute to the preferential binding of topo VI to supercoiled substrates as compared to sheared salmon-sperm DNA.
source: Together, these data indicate that both the KGRR loop and H2TH domain contribute to the preferential binding of topo VI to supercoiled substrates as compared to sheared salmon-sperm DNA, but that neither is solely responsible for this discrimination.
evidence: This conclusion is based on competitive binding experiments with mutants shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Wildtype topo VI binds a stacked-junction substrate nearly 4-fold more tightly than a single 20 bp DNA duplex.
source: Using fluorescence anisotropy, wildtype topo VI was found to bind this substrate nearly 4-fold more tightly than a single 20 bp DNA duplex (Figure 6C, Figure 6—source datas 1–2).
evidence: This finding is supported by fluorescence anisotropy experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Both H2TH mutants show similar increases in affinity for the stacked-junction DNA as seen with native topo VI.
source: Whereas both H2TH mutants showed similar increases in affinity for the stacked-junction DNA as seen with native topo VI, the KGRRAAA mutant showed a clear decrease in affinity for this substrate compared to a 20 bp duplex (and little to no change in affinity for a 20 bp duplex alone, Figure 6C, Figure 6—source datas 1–2).
evidence: This finding is supported by fluorescence anisotropy experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The KGRRAAA mutant shows a clear decrease in affinity for the stacked-junction substrate compared to a 20 bp duplex.
source: Whereas both H2TH mutants showed similar increases in affinity for the stacked-junction DNA as seen with native topo VI, the KGRRAAA mutant showed a clear decrease in affinity for this substrate compared to a 20 bp duplex (and little to no change in affinity for a 20 bp duplex alone, Figure 6C, Figure 6—source datas 1–2).
evidence: This finding is supported by fluorescence anisotropy experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The KGRREEE mutant displays an even more pronounced defect in junction binding than KGRRAAA.
source: The KGRREEE mutant displayed an even more pronounced defect in junction binding.
evidence: This finding is supported by fluorescence anisotropy experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The KGRR loop is implicated in the binding of DNA crossings by topo VI, potentially as a T-segment-sensing element.
source: Collectively, this response implicates the KGRR loop in the binding of DNA crossings by topo VI, potentially as a T-segment-sensing element.
evidence: This conclusion is based on stacked-junction binding experiments with mutants shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The addition of AMPPNP produces a rapid FRET increase in the H2THAAA mutant similar to that of native topo VI, indicating that the ATPase region of this mutant responds to supercoiled DNA and nucleotide in a wildtype-like manner.
source: Although the H2THAAA mutant displayed a lower FRET signal than wild type, both in the presence of supercoiled DNA alone and with supercoiled DNA and nucleotide, the addition of AMPPNP produced a rapid FRET increase in the H2THAAA mutant similar to that of native topo VI, indicating that the ATPase region of this mutant responds to supercoiled DNA and nucleotide in a wildtype-like manner.
evidence: This finding is supported by FRET experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The KGRRAAA mutant initially manifests a higher FRET signal than either wildtype topo VI or the H2THAAA mutant in the presence of supercoiled DNA alone, but the addition of AMPPNP fails to elicit any further increase in FRET.
source: By contrast, the KGRRAAA mutant initially manifested a higher FRET signal than either wildtype topo VI or the H2THAAA mutant in the presence of supercoiled DNA alone; however, the addition of AMPPNP failed to elicit any further increase in FRET (Figure 6D).
evidence: This finding is supported by FRET experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The KGRR loop serves not only as a sensor of DNA crossings, but also as an element that delays ATP turnover until T-segment binding or strand passage has occurred.
source: In this view, the KGRR loop would serve not only as a sensor of DNA crossings, but also as an element that delays ATP turnover until T-segment binding or strand passage has occurred.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined results of FRET and ATPase experiments with KGRR mutants.

claim: Topo VI produced clear cleavage products in the presence of either ATP or AMPPNP on the 70 bp duplex.
source: Although the absence of a T-segment strongly inhibits G-segment scission, topo VI produced clear cleavage products in the presence of either ATP or AMPPNP on the 70 bp duplex.
evidence: This finding is supported by cleavage experiments shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Faint cleavage products were produced from the 60 bp duplex, but only in the presence of AMPPNP.
source: Faint cleavage products were also produced from the 60 bp duplex, but only in the presence of AMPPNP.
evidence: This finding is supported by cleavage experiments shown in Figure 7C.

claim: No cleavage was seen for any condition on the 40 bp duplex.
source: No cleavage was seen for any condition on the 40 bp duplex (Figure 7C).
evidence: This finding is supported by cleavage experiments shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Neither H2TH mutant proved capable of supporting short duplex cleavage.
source: By contrast, neither H2TH mutant proved capable of supporting short duplex cleavage.
evidence: This finding is supported by cleavage experiments shown in Figure 7C.

claim: For a G-segment to bind productively to the Top6A dimer, it ideally should be sufficiently long to engage both the stalk and H2TH regions of Top6B.
source: Collectively, these findings support the idea that for a G-segment to bind productively to the Top6A dimer, it ideally should be sufficiently long to engage both the stalk and H2TH regions of Top6B.
evidence: This conclusion is based on cleavage experiments with different length duplexes and mutants shown in Figure 7C.

claim: G-segment DNAs must engage at least one H2TH domain before strand scission can be triggered.
source: The inability of a 40 bp duplex to support cleavage, even though this DNA binds with higher affinity than a 20 bp duplex and is long enough to reach both Stalk/WKxY regions, suggests G-segment DNAs must engage at least one H2TH domain before strand scission can be triggered.
evidence: This conclusion is based on cleavage experiments with different length duplexes shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The addition of wild-type topo VI alone to labeled DNA leads to a modest FRET increase, indicative of G-segment bending.
source: The addition of wild-type topo VI alone to the labeled DNA led to a modest FRET increase, a result indicative of G-segment bending that accords with prior AFM data (Thomson et al., 2015).
evidence: This finding is supported by FRET-based DNA bending experiments shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Upon adding AMPPNP, FRET efficiency rapidly increases further for labeled DNA incubated with topo VI, indicating that nucleotide-driven dimerization of the ATPase regions leads to additional DNA bending.
source: Upon adding AMPPNP, FRET efficiency rapidly increased further for the labeled DNA incubated with topo VI, or the KGRRAAA or KGRREEE mutants, indicating that nucleotide-driven dimerization of the ATPase regions leads to additional DNA bending.
evidence: This finding is supported by FRET-based DNA bending experiments shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Both Stalk/WKxY mutants produce a FRET increase in the presence of AMPPNP, albeit with substantially slowed kinetics.
source: For their part, both Stalk/WKxY mutants produced a FRET increase in the presence of AMPPNP, albeit with substantially slowed kinetics that likely account for their negligible ATPase activities (Figure 4B).
evidence: This finding is supported by FRET-based DNA bending experiments shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The H2TH mutants do not support any nucleotide-dependent increase in FRET, indicating that Top6B dimerization in these mutants no longer introduces DNA bending to the distal ends of a bound G-segment.
source: By contrast, the H2TH mutants did not support any nucleotide-dependent increase in FRET, indicating that Top6B dimerization in these mutants no longer introduces DNA bending to the distal ends of a bound G-segment.
evidence: This finding is supported by FRET-based DNA bending experiments shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Topo VI engages a G-segment using an extended interface that runs from one H2TH domain to the other.
source: Together, these observations both suggest that topo VI engages a G-segment using an extended interface that runs from one H2TH domain to the other, and that strand scission is stimulated by bending induced by Top6B dimerization.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined results of DNA binding, cleavage, and bending experiments.

claim: Strand scission is stimulated by bending induced by Top6B dimerization.
source: Together, these observations both suggest that topo VI engages a G-segment using an extended interface that runs from one H2TH domain to the other, and that strand scission is stimulated by bending induced by Top6B dimerization.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined results of DNA binding, cleavage, and bending experiments.

claim: There is a feedback mechanism which couples nucleotide turnover to efficient G-segment deformation and cleavage.
source: The observation that the ATPase activity of the H2TH mutants is decoupled from strand passage, yet also substantially impaired when compared to the futile cycling of the KGRR mutants (Figure 4), further suggests that there is a feedback mechanism which couples nucleotide turnover to efficient G-segment deformation and cleavage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of ATPase and strand passage activities of different mutants.
